en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Nissaggiya Section.
Pattavagga 1.
The Training Rule on the Accumulation of Alms Bowls:
Now, venerable ladies, these thirty rules of expiation involving forfeiture come up for recitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six bhikkhunīs were accumulating many almsbowls.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monastery, saw this and complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can these bhikkhunīs store up many bowls, or engage in the trade of bowls, or set up a pottery shop?
The bhikkhunīs heard those people complaining, criticizing, and grumbling.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [and so on]... complained, criticized, and grumbled:
“How can the group of six bhikkhunīs hoard almsbowls? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the group of six bhikkhunīs are hoarding almsbowls?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can the group of six bhikkhunīs amass alms bowls?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, let the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:
“Whichever bhikkhunī should make a hoard of almsbowls, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Whichever bhikkhunī...
Whichever [nun] of such a kind... [as previously described] ...
"a bhikkhunī" ... this is the type of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Bowl" means two kinds of bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl.
There are three sizes for a bowl: a large bowl, a medium bowl, and a small bowl.
The "large" bowl holds half an *āḷhaka* of boiled rice, a fourth part of solid food, and a corresponding amount of curry.
The "medium" bowl—
He takes a *nāḷika* measure of rice, a fourth part of solid food, and a corresponding amount of curry.
A "small" bowl, it is said, takes a *pattha* measure of rice, a fourth part of solid food, and a corresponding amount of curry.
In that case, what is large is not a "received" (patta) [measure], and what is small is not a "received" [measure].
"Should make a hoard" means:
not formally determined (anadhiṭṭhita) and not assigned (avikappita).
"It becomes subject to forfeiture" means that with the rising of the sun, it becomes subject to forfeiture.
It must be forfeited to either the Saṅgha, a group, or a single bhikkhunī.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:

That nun, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged her upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior nuns, having sat down on her haunches and extended her hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“Venerable ladies, this bowl of mine, which has passed the night, is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.”
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
A competent and capable bhikkhunī must receive the confession of the offense.
The relinquished bowl must be returned.
“Let the Saṅgha, noble ladies, hear me.
This bowl, which was subject to relinquishment for the bhikkhunī named so-and-so, has been forfeited to the Saṅgha.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this bowl back to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so.”

That bhikkhunī, having approached several bhikkhunīs, having arranged her upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior bhikkhunīs, having sat down on her haunches and extended her hands in reverential salutation, should speak to them thus:
"Venerable ladies, this bowl of mine has passed the night and is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the venerable ladies.
Having relinquished it, she should confess the offense.
An offense should be accepted from a nun who is competent and experienced.
The bowl that has been relinquished should be given back [with these words]:
"Venerable ladies, let me hear you. [The rest as in the formal act]."
“This bowl, which was subject to forfeiture for the bhikkhunī so-and-so, has been relinquished to the noble ladies.
If it is timely for the noble ladies, may the noble ladies give this bowl back to the bhikkhunī so-and-so.

Then that bhikkhunī, having approached one bhikkhunī, having arranged her upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on her haunches, and having saluted with joined palms, should speak to her thus:
“Venerable lady, this bowl of mine has been kept past the night and is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to you, venerable lady.
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
That nun should accept the offense.
The forfeited bowl should be given back with the words:
"I give this bowl to the noble lady."
If the night has passed and she perceives that it has passed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If the night has passed and she is uncertain, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If the night has passed and she perceives that it has not passed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been formally resolved, but one perceives that it has been resolved, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If it has not been assigned to another, but one perceives that it has been assigned, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been given away, but one perceives that it has been given away, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
Perceiving what is not lost as lost;
perceiving what is not destroyed as destroyed;
perceiving what is unbroken as broken.
If it has not been stolen, but one perceives that it has been stolen, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
If one uses a bowl that has been forfeited without having first relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If the night has not passed, but one perceives that it has passed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If the night has not passed, but she is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If the night has not passed, but she perceives it as not having passed, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If she resolves [to give it away] before dawn, or assigns it, or relinquishes it; if it is lost, destroyed, or broken; if they take it after having stolen it, or take it on trust;
in the case of one who is insane, or one who is a first-offender.
Now at that time, the group-of-six bhikkhunīs did not give back an almsbowl that had been forfeited.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Bhikkhunīs, a forfeited almsbowl must not be withheld; it must be given back."
If she does not give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The first training rule is concluded.
